body.statement:
Under conditional cell-sample independence,
\[
\inf\Pr\{I(m_0,m_1)\subseteq C_n\}\geq1-\gamma,
\]
where the infimum ranges over all maintained bounded cell-outcome laws with the
fixed score laws and compatible means. Whenever
\(Q_n\cap(K_0\times K_1)\neq\varnothing\), \(C_n\) is an attained compact
interval equal to the effect image of all response-surface pairs whose joint
moment vector lies in \(Q_n\). If \(r_d(m_d)>0\) and
\(E_d=\mathbb R^{|J_d|}\) for both arms, and
\(\min_{d,j}n_{dj}\to\infty\), then the Hausdorff distance between \(C_n\) and
\(I(m_0,m_1)\) converges to zero in probability.
body.justification: The theorem covers both endpoints and every value in the sharp set without differentiating a potentially nonsmooth endpoint map.
body.gap: Chernozhukov, Hong, and Tamer give asymptotic criterion inversion, while Qiu and Stoye use an exact-normal approximation and Cattaneo, Titiunik, and Yu infer a point-valued boundary curve from unit-level data.
body.consumer: A sign certificate remains valid after simultaneous sampling uncertainty in every district-level stunting mean is propagated through identification.
body.proof_tex:
\paragraph{Separation of the causal and sampling objects.}
Fix a maintained law \(\mathbb P\) and condition throughout on the fixed positive
cell counts \(n_{dj}\).  Put \(k_d=|J_d|\), so that
\(N=k_0+k_1<\infty\).  The score laws \(\mu_{dj}\) are fixed and known by
\(\texttt{ass:known-cell-score-laws}\), whereas the sampling randomness below
comes only from the outcomes \(Y_{dji}\in[0,1]\).  The causal object is
\(\tau_B\), and, by \(\texttt{thm:sharp-mean-information-set}\), its sharp
mean-information set at the population moment vector is
\[
 I(m_0,m_1)
 =
 [\,L_1(m_1)-U_0(m_0),\,
     U_1(m_1)-L_0(m_0)\,].
\]
Thus \(I(m_0,m_1)\) is not defined by the confidence construction.  The random
set \(C_n\) is instead the inversion, defined in
\(\texttt{def:whole-set-confidence}\), of the observed-law confidence box
\(Q_n\) from \(\texttt{def:confidence-box}\).  The polygonal boundary,
boundary normalization, cell support, and compatibility conditions needed for
the displayed causal characterization are precisely those invoked by the
frozen sharp-set theorem.

\paragraph{Simultaneous finite-sample coverage.}
Suppose first that \(N\geq1\).  For any \((d,j)\), conditional independence in
\(\texttt{ass:cell-sample-independence}\), the support
\(0\leq Y_{dji}\leq1\), and the frozen bounded-sum Hoeffding lemma give
\[
 \mathbb P\!\left\{
   \widehat m_{dj}-m_{dj}>e_{dj}
 \right\}
 \leq
 \exp\{-2n_{dj}e_{dj}^{\,2}\}.
\]
Applying the same lemma to \(-Y_{dji}\in[-1,0]\) gives the lower-tail
inequality.  Hence
\[
 \mathbb P\!\left\{
   |\widehat m_{dj}-m_{dj}|>e_{dj}
 \right\}
 \leq
 2\exp\{-2n_{dj}e_{dj}^{\,2}\}
 =
 \frac{\gamma}{N},
\]
where the equality uses
\(e_{dj}^{\,2}=\log(2N/\gamma)/(2n_{dj})\), the positivity
\(n_{dj}\geq1\), and \(0<\gamma<1\).  A union bound over the \(N\) cells
therefore yields
\[
 \mathbb P\!\left\{
   |\widehat m_{dj}-m_{dj}|\leq e_{dj}
   \text{ for every }d,j
 \right\}
 \geq1-\gamma.                                      \tag{1}
\]
Every population mean \(m_{dj}\) lies in \([0,1]\), since it is the mean of a
\([0,1]\)-valued outcome.  Consequently clipping each coordinate interval to
\([0,1]\) does not remove \(m_{dj}\), and the event in (1) implies
\((m_0,m_1)\in Q_n\).  Compatibility
\(\texttt{ass:mean-compatibility}\) gives
\((m_0,m_1)\in K_0\times K_1\); thus the union defining \(C_n\) contains
\(I(m_0,m_1)\) on that event.  If \(N=0\), there are no coordinate
inequalities, the empty-coordinate product contains the unique empty moment
vector with probability one, and the same inclusion is immediate.  The
argument did not use any feature of \(\mathbb P\) beyond the declared
independence, support, means, and fixed score laws.  Taking the infimum over all
maintained laws therefore proves
\[
 \inf_{\mathbb P}
 \mathbb P\{I(m_0,m_1)\subseteq C_n\}\geq1-\gamma.
                                                               \tag{2}
\]

\paragraph{Compact interval and exact effect image.}
For completeness, first verify the compactness used here directly from the
primitive class.  The set \(S\) is compact by
\(\texttt{ass:polygonal-score-support}\).  Any sequence in
\(\mathcal F_d\) is uniformly bounded in \([0,1]\) and has the common
modulus \(M_d\|x-y\|_2\) by \(\texttt{def:surface-class}\).  Choose a finite
\(1/\ell\)-net of \(S\) for each positive integer \(\ell\).  Successive
subsequence extraction on the finite nets, followed by a diagonal choice,
produces a subsequence whose values converge at every point in the union of
the nets.  If \(x\) is within \(1/\ell\) of a net point \(x_\ell\), then for
two functions in this subsequence,
\[
 |g^{(r)}_d(x)-g^{(s)}_d(x)|
 \leq
 2M_d/\ell+
 |g^{(r)}_d(x_\ell)-g^{(s)}_d(x_\ell)|.
\]
First choosing \(\ell\) large and then \(r,s\) large shows that the subsequence
is uniformly Cauchy.  Its uniform limit is continuous, takes values in
\([0,1]\), and remains \(M_d\)-Lipschitz after passing to the limit in the
defining inequality.  Thus \(\mathcal F_d\) is compact in the uniform norm.
It is convex because both its range constraints and Lipschitz inequalities
are preserved by convex combinations.

Each \(\mu_{dj}\) is a probability measure, and \(\nu\) is a probability
measure by \(\texttt{ass:boundary-weight-normalization}\).  Therefore
\[
 \left|\int_S(g_d-\widetilde g_d)\,d\mu_{dj}\right|
 \leq\|g_d-\widetilde g_d\|_\infty,
 \qquad
 \left|\int_B(g_d-\widetilde g_d)\,d\nu\right|
 \leq\|g_d-\widetilde g_d\|_\infty.                 \tag{3}
\]
So the moment maps and the boundary-effect map are continuous.

Define the random feasible surface set
\[
 \mathcal R_n
 =
 \left\{(g_0,g_1)\in\mathcal F_0\times\mathcal F_1:
       (A_0g_0,A_1g_1)\in Q_n\right\}
\]
and the continuous linear effect map
\[
 T(g_0,g_1)=\int_B(g_1-g_0)\,d\nu.
\]
Because \(Q_n\) is a closed convex box, (3) shows that
\(\mathcal R_n\) is a closed convex subset of the compact convex product
\(\mathcal F_0\times\mathcal F_1\).  Moreover,
\(\mathcal R_n\neq\varnothing\) exactly when
\(Q_n\cap(K_0\times K_1)\neq\varnothing\): the forward implication follows
from \(\texttt{def:moment-body}\), and the reverse implication follows by
choosing, independently for each arm, a surface in the nonempty fiber defining
membership in \(K_d=A_d(\mathcal F_d)\).

When this intersection is nonempty, \(T(\mathcal R_n)\) is therefore a
nonempty compact convex subset of \(\mathbb R\), hence an attained compact
interval.  Partitioning \(\mathcal R_n\) by its joint moment vector gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 T(\mathcal R_n)
 &=
 \bigcup_{(q_0,q_1)\in Q_n\cap(K_0\times K_1)}
 \left\{
   \int_B(g_1-g_0)\,d\nu:
   g_d\in\mathcal F_d,\ A_dg_d=q_d
 \right\} \\
 &=
 \bigcup_{(q_0,q_1)\in Q_n\cap(K_0\times K_1)}
 I(q_0,q_1)
 =C_n.                                                   \tag{4}
\end{aligned}
\]
The second equality is exactly the fiberwise sharpness conclusion of
\(\texttt{thm:sharp-mean-information-set}\), including attainment of every
value.  Equation (4) proves both the asserted effect-image identity and the
attainment of the endpoints of \(C_n\).  The unrestricted dual representation
in \(\texttt{thm:clipping-transport-dual}\) is consequently a valid
observed-law endpoint computation for every fixed compatible fiber, but no
differentiability of that dual value is used below.

\paragraph{A local modulus for the arm endpoints.}
We derive the continuity required for consistency rather than assuming it.
Fix an arm \(d\).  Convexity of \(\mathcal F_d\), linearity of \(A_d\), and
linearity of the boundary integral imply that \(U_d\) is concave on \(K_d\):
if \(q,q'\in K_d\), maxima are attained by the preceding compactness argument,
and mixing their maximizers is feasible at
\(\alpha q+(1-\alpha)q'\) and attains
\(\alpha U_d(q)+(1-\alpha)U_d(q')\).  Similarly \(L_d\) is convex.
The range restriction and \(\nu(B)=1\) imply
\[
 0\leq U_d(q)\leq1,\qquad 0\leq L_d(q)\leq1
 \quad(q\in K_d).                                      \tag{5}
\]

Now impose the rank and interior conditions in the theorem:
\[
 E_d=\mathbb R^{k_d},\qquad r_d(m_d)>0.                \tag{6}
\]
Choose once and for all a number \(R_d\) with
\(0<R_d<r_d(m_d)\).  By the definition in
\(\texttt{def:relative-interior-radius}\), the feasible-radius set is
downward closed, so
\[
 m_d+R_d\mathbb B_{\mathbb R^{k_d}}\subseteq K_d.       \tag{7}
\]
For \(q_d\in K_d\), set \(t=\|q_d-m_d\|_2\).  If \(t>0\), the point
\[
 z_-=m_d-\frac{R_d}{t}(q_d-m_d)
\]
belongs to \(K_d\) by (7), and
\[
 m_d=\frac{R_d}{R_d+t}q_d+\frac{t}{R_d+t}z_-.
\]
Concavity of \(U_d\) and (5) then give
\[
 U_d(m_d)
 \geq
 \frac{R_d}{R_d+t}U_d(q_d)
 +\frac{t}{R_d+t}U_d(z_-)
 \geq
 \frac{R_d}{R_d+t}U_d(q_d),
\]
and hence
\[
 U_d(q_d)-U_d(m_d)\leq\frac{t}{R_d}.                  \tag{8}
\]
If \(t<R_d\), the triangle inequality and (7) also give
\[
 q_d+(R_d-t)\mathbb B_{\mathbb R^{k_d}}\subseteq K_d.
\]
Applying (8) with center \(q_d\), radius \(R_d-t\), and comparison point
\(m_d\) yields
\[
 U_d(m_d)-U_d(q_d)\leq\frac{t}{R_d-t}.                \tag{9}
\]
Combining (8)--(9), for \(t\leq R_d/2\),
\[
 |U_d(q_d)-U_d(m_d)|\leq\frac{2t}{R_d}.               \tag{10}
\]
Since \(1-L_d\) is concave and takes values in \([0,1]\) by (5), exactly the
same argument gives
\[
 |L_d(q_d)-L_d(m_d)|\leq\frac{2t}{R_d}
 \quad\text{whenever }t\leq R_d/2.                    \tag{11}
\]
This exposes the only rank requirement: (6) makes the relative ball an ambient
Euclidean ball.  No matrix inversion, density positivity, treatment-overlap
division, or additional boundary regularity is used in (8)--(11).

\paragraph{Hausdorff consistency.}
Let
\[
 \Delta_{d,n}
 =
 \|\widehat m_d-m_d\|_2
 +\sqrt{k_d}\max_{j\in J_d}e_{dj},
\]
with the second term interpreted as zero when \(k_d=0\).  Boundedness gives
\(\operatorname{Var}(\widehat m_{dj})\leq1/(4n_{dj})\): indeed
\(\operatorname{Var}(Y_{dji})\leq
\mathbb E[(Y_{dji}-1/2)^2]\leq1/4\), and independence gives the variance of
the sample mean.  Therefore
\[
 \mathbb E\|\widehat m_d-m_d\|_2^2
 =
 \sum_{j\in J_d}\operatorname{Var}(\widehat m_{dj})
 \leq
 \sum_{j\in J_d}\frac{1}{4n_{dj}}
 \longrightarrow0,                                   \tag{12}
\]
where the limit uses finiteness of the fixed set \(J_d\) and
\(\min_{d,j}n_{dj}\to\infty\).  Markov's inequality applied to the squared
norm shows
\(\|\widehat m_d-m_d\|_2\to0\) in probability.  The same sample-size limit,
with fixed \(N\) and \(0<\gamma<1\), gives
\(\max_j e_{dj}\to0\).  Hence
\[
 \Delta_{d,n}\ \xrightarrow{\mathbb P}\ 0.             \tag{13}
\]

Every coordinate of \(\widehat m_d\) belongs to its clipped confidence
interval because \(\widehat m_{dj}\in[0,1]\).  On
\(\{\|\widehat m_d-m_d\|_2<R_d\}\), (7) gives
\(\widehat m_d\in K_d\); thus \(Q_n\cap(K_0\times K_1)\) is nonempty with
probability tending to one.  Moreover, for every
\(q_d\in Q_n\cap K_d\),
\[
 \|q_d-m_d\|_2
 \leq
 \|q_d-\widehat m_d\|_2+\|\widehat m_d-m_d\|_2
 \leq
 \sqrt{k_d}\max_j e_{dj}
 +\|\widehat m_d-m_d\|_2
 =\Delta_{d,n}.                                       \tag{14}
\]

Write
\[
 a=L_1(m_1)-U_0(m_0),\qquad
 b=U_1(m_1)-L_0(m_0).
\]
On the event
\(\Delta_{d,n}\leq R_d/2\) for both arms, (10), (11), and (14) show, uniformly
over all \((q_0,q_1)\in Q_n\cap(K_0\times K_1)\), that
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \left|
   \{L_1(q_1)-U_0(q_0)\}-a
 \right|
 &\leq
 \frac{2\Delta_{1,n}}{R_1}
 +\frac{2\Delta_{0,n}}{R_0},\\
 \left|
   \{U_1(q_1)-L_0(q_0)\}-b
 \right|
 &\leq
 \frac{2\Delta_{1,n}}{R_1}
 +\frac{2\Delta_{0,n}}{R_0}.                         \tag{15}
\end{aligned}
\]
By (4), the lower endpoint of \(C_n\) is the minimum of the first expression
in braces over the displayed compact moment set, and its upper endpoint is
the maximum of the second expression in braces.  Hence (15) bounds the
absolute error of each endpoint by
\[
 \zeta_n=
 \frac{2\Delta_{1,n}}{R_1}
 +\frac{2\Delta_{0,n}}{R_0}
 \xrightarrow{\mathbb P}0.                            \tag{16}
\]
For two nonempty compact real intervals, Hausdorff distance is the maximum of
the absolute differences of their corresponding endpoints.  Equations
(13)--(16), together with the probability tending to one of nonemptiness,
therefore imply
\[
 d_{\mathrm H}\!\left(C_n,I(m_0,m_1)\right)
 \xrightarrow{\mathbb P}0.
\]
If Hausdorff distance is extended arbitrarily, for example by \(+\infty\),
on the vanishing event that \(C_n\) is empty, the same convergence statement
holds.  This proves all three assertions.
